title: Symbols and Symbol Literals
subtopics: Symbol use as identifiers and keys
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of symbols and symbol literals in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply symbols and symbol literals in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to symbol use as identifiers and keys and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Symbols and Symbol Literals through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding symbols and symbol literals helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Symbols and Symbol Literals helps you reason about symbol creation. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Symbol creation. Then connect it to Symbol identity. The remaining syllabus points—Symbol use as identifiers and keys—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports symbols and symbol literals. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for symbols and symbol literals using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Symbol use as identifiers and keys), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain symbols and symbol literals, identify its place in data types, literals, and operators, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
